subject: botany
question_text: Explain the zwitterionic form of an amino acid.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Botany Fastrack, Chapter 10 Biomolecules, book p.26, VSAQ 3. The book prints 'P^H' (scan noise for pH) and 'converting NH2 to NH3+ & COOH to COO-'; the chemistry is correct and is written out here in full symbols. The book does not say where this form dominates — the standard point (neutral pH) is added. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the board-paper back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun; 'not checked' here means exactly that, never 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The two groups ionise
lines: An amino acid carries an amino group –NH₂
and a carboxyl group –COOH on the same
Depending on the pH of the solution:
steps.why: The two groups behave in opposite ways: the amino group is basic and accepts a proton, the carboxyl group is acidic and gives one away. That is how one amino acid can carry both charges at once.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two changes. The amino group GAINS a proton; the carboxyl group LOSES one.
Leaving out the charges. –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ must be written with their signs.
steps.memory_tip: Amino group takes a proton and turns positive; carboxyl group gives one away and turns negative.
steps.margin_note: Write both changes with arrows. The two ionisation lines carry this mark.

steps.label: Definition of the zwitterion

lines.text: Zwitterion = one positive + one negative charge, net charge zero

lines: The amino acid then carries equal positive
and negative charges on the same molecule.
This dipolar form is called the zwitterionic
form. It is the usual form at neutral pH.
steps.why: 'Zwitter' means double, so the name records that the molecule carries two opposite charges at the same time. The charges are equal, so the molecule as a whole is neutral.
common_mistakes: Writing that the zwitterion has a net positive or net negative charge. The net charge is zero.
Calling it a neutral molecule with no charges. It has both charges; they cancel.
steps.memory_tip: Zwitter means double — double charge, zero total.
steps.margin_note: The words 'no net charge' must appear. That is what the examiner ticks.

insider_note: The mark is lost most often for writing the charges without signs. Write –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ exactly.
